what_its_for: Ciprofloxacin is an antibiotic used to treat many types of bacterial infections, including urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney infections, skin infections, respiratory infections, bone and joint infections, and certain types of diarrhea. It works by stopping the growth of bacteria. Remember, this medicine will NOT work for colds, flu, or other viral infections.
how_to_take: Take ciprofloxacin exactly as your doctor prescribed — do not skip doses or stop early, even if you feel better. You can take regular tablets with or without food. Swallow extended-release (XR) tablets whole — do not crush, split, or chew them. Drink plenty of water and fluids while taking this medicine. If you take an antacid, calcium supplement, iron pill, multivitamin, or any dairy product (like milk or yogurt), take ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours BEFORE or 6 hours AFTER those items, as they can block the medicine from working properly.
dosing: Your dose depends on the type and severity of your infection. Common doses for adults range from 250 mg to 750 mg taken every 12 hours (twice a day), or 500 mg to 1000 mg of the extended-release form once daily. Treatment usually lasts 3 to 14 days, but some infections may require longer. Always follow the exact dose and schedule your doctor or pharmacist gave you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ciprofloxacin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the medicine away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep it out of reach of children. Do not use the medicine after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids, calcium-fortified juices, dairy products (milk, yogurt, cheese), iron supplements, or multivitamins within 2 hours before or 6 hours after your dose. Avoid excessive sun exposure and tanning beds — ciprofloxacin can make your skin much more sensitive to sunlight, increasing your risk of sunburn. Use sunscreen and protective clothing when going outdoors. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or confused. Limit caffeine intake, as ciprofloxacin can increase its effects, causing jitteriness or a fast heartbeat. Avoid strenuous exercise during treatment, as this medicine may rarely cause tendon damage.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: sudden pain, swelling, or tearing in a tendon (especially in the heel, shoulder, or hand); numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms or legs; severe or persistent diarrhea (watery or bloody); fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat; mental or mood changes such as confusion, anxiety, hallucinations, or thoughts of hurting yourself; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); difficulty breathing or swallowing; or signs of a severe allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat. Also call your doctor if your symptoms are not improving after a few days.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 1 to 3 days of starting ciprofloxacin. However, it is very important to finish the entire course of antibiotics even if you feel completely well. Stopping early can allow the bacteria to come back stronger and harder to treat.
special_populations: Children and Teenagers: Ciprofloxacin is generally not the first choice for children and teenagers because it may affect developing joints and cartilage. It is used in young patients only when necessary and prescribed by a doctor. Pregnant Women: Talk to your doctor before taking ciprofloxacin if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Breastfeeding Mothers: Ciprofloxacin passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby. Consult your doctor about the safest option for you and your baby. Older Adults (65+): Older adults may be at a higher risk for tendon problems, especially if they also take steroid medications (like prednisone). Report any tendon pain or swelling to your doctor immediately. Kidney Problems: If you have kidney disease, your doctor may lower your dose. Make sure your doctor knows about any kidney conditions before you start this medicine.
